newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court clarifies voting rights standard.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court clarifies voting rights standard.

text.p: The Supreme Court handed the Justice Department a defeat Monday by making it harder for federal officials to reject proposed changes in district boundaries that might hurt minority voting power.

The high court, by a 7-2 vote in a case from Louisiana, clarified the standard the Justice Department's civil rights unit should apply to review changes state or local governments make in district boundaries or other voting procedures.

Under section 5 of the federal voting rights law, many state or local governments must receive pre-clearance from the Justice Department by showing a proposed change has no discriminatory purpose or effect. The law says the change may not leave minority voters worse off than they had been.

But section 2 of the law, which applies nationwide, bars any voting practice that has a discriminatory effect, without regard to purpose. It prohibits any voting practice that would dilute minority voting strength.
The Justice Department, since a 1987 regulation, has taken the view that any practice that violates section 2 is automatically disqualified from pre-clearance under section 5.
But Justice Sandra Day O'Connor wrote for the court majority that pre-clearance may not be denied solely on the basis that a new voting practice violates section 2.
"This court has consistently understood (the two sections) to combat different evils and, accordingly to impose very different duties upon the states," she said.

The justices set aside the decision of a three-judge federal court and told it to restudy a Bossier Parish school board redistricting plan that included no majority-black districts, even though 20 percent of the population is black.
